answer.rationale: The primary supply contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renewal and the assembly line is at 94% with zero buffer. Memory c1 tells me renewing with the incumbent kept integration stable with no migration work or delivery interruption — that is exactly the risk profile I cannot afford to disturb under the current constraint. Memory c6 tells me a multi-year commitment with the incumbent can unlock volume pricing and cut unit cost without narrowing service scope, which is the only lever that directly addresses finance's 18% cost-cut mandate within this single decision window. I want to verify c2 to confirm the low-cost vendor's actual performance record, because if its cost advantage is large enough it might tempt a switch — but the absence of buffer and the 14-day expiry make any onboarding risk unacceptable this cycle. I want to verify c6 to confirm the multi-year volume-pricing mechanism and its terms, since that is the specific instrument I intend to negotiate into the renewal to hit the cost target. Adding a second source (c3) or deferring (c5) are both viable in normal cycles but fail the primary objective here: c3 exceeds my single-decision capacity and adds integration risk with no immediate cost relief; c5 leaves the contract lapsed with the line already at 94% and no buffer. Negotiating terms (c4) is folded into the renewal itself as the vehicle for the multi-year volume commitment. Therefore: renew the incumbent, structured as a multi-year commitment to capture volume pricing, and embed a renegotiation pass modeled on c4's benchmarking approach to squeeze additional margin and better payment terms, all within the single decision slot.
